questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

A number of students _______ participating in the annual sports meet.
options_en: is
be
has
are
options_hi: is
be
has
are
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D)- Replace the blank with "are".

Rule/Concept: "A Number of" vs. "The Number of" This is a high-frequency exception in competitive exams. Unlike "A group of," the phrase "A number of" functions as a plural quantifier (meaning "many" or "several"). Therefore, it always takes a plural verb.

Why it is Plural:

A number of: This phrase is used to mean "some" or "many." The focus is on the individual students within the group, making the subject plural.

The number of: This phrase refers to the specific total or the numerical value itself (e.g., "The number of students is 50"). Since a "total" is a single figure, it takes a singular verb.

Examples:

A number of workers have gone on strike. (Plural)

The number of workers on strike is twenty. (Singular)

Corrected Sentence: A number of students are participating in the annual sports meet.

In a sentence involving two nouns, we use This to refer to the noun mentioned last (the one closest to the pronoun) and That to refer to the noun mentioned first (the one farther away).

questions.q_en:
Renewable energy is often presented as an uncomplicated remedy to the twin crises of climate change and energy insecurity. Governments announce ambitious targets, corporations highlight sustainability commitments, and public discourse treats renewables as an inevitable successor to fossil fuels. Yet this narrative of inevitability conceals a more complex reality. Transitioning to renewable energy is not merely a technological substitution but a structural transformation involving land use, grid stability, economic redistribution, and political negotiation. Ignoring these dimensions risks replacing one form of dependency with another. One persistent challenge lies in intermittency. Solar and wind energy, while abundant, are not continuously available, requiring storage systems or backup infrastructure. Although technological advances have reduced costs, large-scale storage remains economically and logistically constrained. As a result, renewable integration often relies on conventional energy sources during periods of low generation. This dependence complicates claims of energy independence and exposes the limits of viewing renewables as a standalone solution.

Social and environmental trade-offs further complicate the transition. Large renewable projects demand vast land areas, sometimes displacing communities or disrupting local ecosystems. Ironically, projects designed to mitigate environmental harm can generate localized ecological and social resistance. When decision-making excludes affected populations, renewable energy risks replicating the extractive logic historically associated with fossil fuels—only under a different moral banner.

The long-term success of renewable energy, therefore, depends less on technological optimism and more on institutional capacity. Transparent governance, adaptive grid management, and equitable distribution of costs and benefits are critical. Without these, renewable energy may expand in capacity yet fall short in legitimacy, provoking resistance that slows the very transition it seeks to accelerate.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The infrastructure of the new smart city
is significantly more advanced and sustainable
than the old industrial township.
No Error
options_hi: The infrastructure of the new smart city
is significantly more advanced and sustainable
than the old industrial township.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

Replace “than the old” with “than that of the old”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Illogical Comparison (That of / Those of)

In English, comparisons must be made between comparable entities. You cannot compare an attribute of one thing (e.g., the infrastructure) directly to the thing itself (e.g., the township). To avoid this "illogical comparison," we use the demonstrative pronouns "that of" (for singular nouns) or "those of" (for plural nouns) to refer back to the attribute being compared.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the subject is "The infrastructure" (of the new smart city). As the sentence currently stands in Part C, it compares the "infrastructure" to the "old industrial township" itself. This is logically incorrect; we must compare the infrastructure of the new city with the infrastructure of the old township. Since "infrastructure" is singular, we must use "that of" to represent it in the second half of the comparison.

Corrected Sentence –

The infrastructure of the new smart city is significantly more advanced and sustainable than that of the old industrial township.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 : The climate of Hyderabad is better than that of Chennai. (Comparing climate to climate). ✅

Example 2 : The streets of London are wider than those of Mumbai. (Comparing plural streets to streets). ✅

Example 3 : Her performance in the mock test was superior to that of any other student. ✅

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option B

👉 Replace “was because” with “was that”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Redundancy – The reason... that (Polarity of Cause)

In formal English, the phrase "The reason" itself functions as a noun that introduces a cause. Using the conjunction "because" (which also indicates cause) in the same sentence creates a redundancy error. This is known as a superfluous expression.

The Rule: The noun phrase "The reason" must be followed by the conjunction "that" to complete the explanation.

The Trap: Using "The reason... is because" is common in casual speech but is a major error

✅ Corrected Sentence

The reason the negotiations collapsed was that neither party was willing to compromise.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

The "Why" Factor: Even if the sentence says "The reason why...", the rule remains the same—it must still be followed by "that," never "because."

Key Indicator: Whenever you see "The reason" at the start of a sentence, immediately scan for "because" later in the sentence to spot the error.

questions.solution_en:
Blank 1: entrust... with / Blank 2: entrust... to

The "Entrust" Structural Rule

Formula: Entrust + [Person] + With + [Object].

Formula: Entrust + [Object] + To + [Person].

Application to the Given Question

"...to entrust a young guardian [1] _________ the care... than to entrust them [2] _________ a state-run institution."

First Blank: The word immediately following the verb is "a young guardian" (the caretaker). Since we are placing the responsibility into their hands, we use with.

Second Blank: The word immediately following the verb is "them" (the orphans, i.e., the "people to be cared for"). Since we are handing the orphans over to the institution, we use to.
questions.solution_hi:
Blank 1: entrust... with / Blank 2: entrust... to

The "Entrust" Structural Rule

Formula: Entrust + [Person] + With + [Object].

Formula: Entrust + [Object] + To + [Person].

Application to the Given Question

"...to entrust a young guardian [1] _________ the care... than to entrust them [2] _________ a state-run institution."

First Blank: The word immediately following the verb is "a young guardian" (the caretaker). Since we are placing the responsibility into their hands, we use with.

Second Blank: The word immediately following the verb is "them" (the orphans, i.e., the "people to be cared for"). Since we are handing the orphans over to the institution, we use to.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “most safest” with “safest”.

Rule/Concept: Avoid “More/Most” with Comparative or Superlative Adjectives

Comparative adjectives (better, superior, safer) already express a comparison, so using “more” before them is incorrect.

Superlative adjectives (best, highest, safest) already express the extreme, so using “most” before them is redundant and wrong.

Corrected Sentence - Out of all the proposals submitted to the corporate strategy team over the past six months, the one presented last week is the safest option according to the comprehensive risk assessment and feasibility study conducted by the consultants.

More Examples for Clarity -

She is the best candidate for the position. (Not “most best”).

This route is safer than the other alternatives. (Not “more safer”).

Of all the solutions proposed, this is the highest quality option. (Not “most highest quality”).

Incorrect Usage -

He is more better than his colleague.

This is the most safest route to the destination.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

Identify if the adjective is already comparative or superlative.

Never add more before comparatives or most before superlatives.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

📌 Rule / Concept: Modal Verb “Ought to” in Passive Voice (Ought to + be + V³)

“Ought to” functions as a semi-modal verb and follows a fixed passive structure: Ought to + be + V³

Unlike simple modals (can, may, must), “ought” is always followed by “to.” In passive voice, the structure becomes: Object + ought to be + V³

The modal meaning (moral duty / advisability) remains unchanged.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option B

👉 Replace “between” with “from”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Prepositional Pairings – From... to vs. Between... and

In English grammar, prepositions used to express a range or duration must follow a specific correlative pairing. Using a mismatched combination is a frequent error in high-level competitive exams.

From... to: This pair is used to indicate a movement, range, or period starting at one point and ending at another.

Between... and: This pair is used to specify the interval or space separating two distinct points.

✅ Corrected Sentence: The training programme will be conducted from 1st March to 30th April across all regional offices.

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: The price of the stock fluctuated from ₹500 to ₹550.

Example 2: You can find the manager in his office from Monday to Friday.

❌ Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 ❌: The seminar is scheduled between 2 PM to 4 PM. (Should be from... to)

Wrong example 2 ❌: He travelled between Delhi to Mumbai by train. (Should be from... to)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “is” with “be”.

📌 Rule / Concept: The Mandative Subjunctive (Passive Voice)

The Present Subjunctive mood is triggered by verbs of formal motion, demand, or requirement (such as move, demand, insist, mandate). When the action in the "that-clause" is passive (the subject is receiving the action), we must use the base form of the verb "to be" (be) followed by the past participle (V3). Even if the subject is singular (the member nation), the indicative forms "is," "am," or "are" are strictly prohibited in this mood.

💢 Application to the Given Question - The verb moved (in the sense of making a formal parliamentary motion or proposal) requires the subjunctive mood in the following clause. The member nation is the one being suspended (passive voice). Therefore, the indicative verb is must be replaced by the subjunctive base form be.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ The chairman moved that the meeting be adjourned.

Example 2 ✅ It was proposed that the old building be demolished.

Example 3 ✅ The advocate moved that the prisoner be released on bail.

but, the rural masses
have the habit of saving.

in the banking sector,
but, the rural masses
have the habit of saving.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option C

👉 Replace “but” with “because”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Cause vs. Contrast (Polarity of Logic)

In conjunctions, choosing the right word depends on the logical relationship between the two statements.

But: Used for Contrast (Positive statement ↔ Negative statement).

Because: Used for Cause/Reason (Fact ➔ Explanation for that fact/ Positive + Positive).

 

✅ Correct Sentence: "There is growth potential in the banking sector because the rural masses have the habit of saving."

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “laden” with “loaded”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Loaded vs. Laden -

Loaded (Functional/Mechanical): Used when a vehicle, container, or device is filled with a specific cargo or contents.

Key Contexts: Trucks, ships, planes, guns, cameras, or even data.

Example: The loaded gun was kept in the safe.

Laden (Descriptive/Natural): Used to describe a state of being "weighed down" or heavily burdened. It carries a more literary or physical connotation of "hanging heavy."

Key Contexts: Tree branches (fruit/snow), people (carrying bundles/bags), or abstract burdens (emotions/guilt).

Example: The orchard was laden with ripe peaches.

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the object is a freighter (a cargo ship). Because a ship is a commercial vessel designed to carry a specific "load" of cargo (hazardous chemicals), the word "loaded" is the precise technical term required.

in his private studio passionately

No Error

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “in his private studio passionately” with “passionately in his private studio”.

Rule / Concept: The M-P-T Rule (Sequence of Adverbs)

When a sentence contains multiple adverbs or adverbial phrases—specifically Adverb of Manner (how), Adverb of Place (where), and Adverb of Time (when)—they must follow a specific chronological order: Manner → Place → Time (M-P-T).

Application to the Given Question

"...painted in his private studio passionately every morning..."

In this sentence, we have three distinct adverbial components:

  1. Place: in his private studio

  2. Manner: passionately

  3. Time: every morning

The current structure follows a P-M-T order, which is grammatically incorrect. According to the MPT rule, the adverb of manner ("passionately") must come first, followed by the place ("in his private studio"), and finally the time ("every morning").

Corrected Sentence

The legendary artist painted passionately in his private studio every morning before the sunrise.



More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: She danced gracefully (M) on the stage (P) last night (T). ✅

Example 2: He spoke earnestly (M) at the meeting (P) this morning (T). ✅

Example 3: The children played happily (M) in the garden (P) all afternoon (T). ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1: She danced last night gracefully on the stage. (T-M-P) ❌

Wrong example 2: He spoke at the meeting earnestly this morning. (P-M-T) ❌

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • The MPT Formula: Memorize the acronym MPT as if it were a mathematical formula for sentence construction.

  • Verb of Movement Exception: If the verb indicates movement (e.g., go, come, arrive, reach), the order often shifts to P-M-T (e.g., "He went to Delhi [P] by train [M] yesterday [T]"). However, for standard action verbs, stick strictly to M-P-T.



Some verbs don’t follow MPT rule.

(go, come, arrive, reach etc.)

questions.solution_en:
Hearsay (अफवाह)/(सुनी सुनाई बात) - Information that is received from other people and not directly from personal knowledge or experience; gossip or unverified information.

Audible (सुना जा सकने वाला) - Able to be heard; loud enough to be heard.

Rumour (अफवाह)/(ख़बर) - A currently circulating story or report of uncertain or doubtful truth; gossip or speculation.

Callous (कठोर)/(निर्दयी) - Showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others; emotionally hardened or unfeeling.

Fatuous (मूर्ख)/(बेवकूफ) - Silly and pointless; lacking in seriousness or intelligence; foolish or inane.

questions.q_en:
Identify the grammatical function of the highlighted phrase.

The speaker addressed the audience with remarkable confidence and clarity.
questions.q_hi:
Identify the grammatical function of the highlighted phrase.

The speaker addressed the audience with remarkable confidence and clarity.
options_en: Functioning as a noun
Functioning as an adjective
Functioning as an adverb
Functioning as a subject
options_hi: Functioning as a noun
Functioning as an adjective
Functioning as an adverb
Functioning as a subject
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Functioning as an adverb

Explanation: An adverb phrase functions like an adverb and modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. It tells how, when, where, or to what extent something happens.

The highlighted phrase:

“with remarkable confidence and clarity” modifies the verb “addressed.”

addressed how? → with remarkable confidence and clarity

Therefore, the phrase functions as an adverb.

Why other options are incorrect:

A) A noun functions as a subject, object, or complement. The phrase is not naming anything here.

B) An adjective modifies a noun/pronoun, but the phrase modifies the verb “addressed.”

D) The subject of the sentence is “The speaker,” not the highlighted phrase.
